entry.summary: This paper presents an open-source, modular hardware-triggered time-synchronization circuit for roadside multi-lidar, multi-camera systems, using a lidar sync pulse as reference to generate independently programmable time-delayed camera triggers. It enables accurate temporal alignment for reliable perception in dense urban traffic.

entry.title: A Systematic Review of ECG Arrhythmia Classification: Adherence to Standards, Fair Evaluation, and Embedded Feasibility

author.name: Guilherme Silva, Pedro Silva, Gladston Moreira, Vander Freitas, Jadson Gertrudes, Eduardo Luz

entry.summary: A systematic review of ECG arrhythmia classification studies from 2017-2024, emphasizing standardization, fair evaluation protocols, and feasibility on embedded devices like pacemakers and wearables. It highlights how many studies ignore deployment constraints and reproducibility standards.

entry.title: On inferring cumulative constraints

author.name: Konstantin Sidorov

entry.summary: This work presents a preprocessing method that infers additional cumulative constraints in scheduling by treating them as linear inequalities over occupancy vectors, discovering task covers, and lifting the inequalities. Experiments on standard RCPSP benchmarks show reduced solving slowdowns.

entry.title: Normalisation and Initialisation Strategies for Graph Neural Networks in Blockchain Anomaly Detection

author.name: Dang Sy Duy and Nguyen Duy Chien and Kapil Dev and Jeff Nijsse

entry.summary: A systematic ablation of weight initialization and normalization strategies across GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE for anti-money-laundering detection on the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset. It finds these choices are strongly architecture-dependent.

entry.title: Energy-Efficient Information Representation in MNIST Classification Using Biologically Inspired Learning

author.name: Patrick Stricker, Florian R\"ohrbein, and Andreas Knoblauch

entry.summary: The paper analyzes a biologically inspired learning rule emulating brain structural plasticity, using information-theoretic tools to show it prevents overparameterization on MNIST classification. It frames efficiency gains against the environmental costs of large models.

entry.title: AnovaX: A Local, Multi-Agent Voice Assistant with LLM Planning, Typed Executors, and Adaptive Recovery

author.name: Raunak B Sinha

entry.summary: AnovaX is a local-first, multi-agent desktop voice assistant that runs entirely on-device, using a Gemini planner to emit JSON tool-call plans, a whitelist/denylist safety layer, typed child agents, and an adaptive recovery loop. It treats the desktop as its action surface for privacy-preserving automation.

entry.title: A Transportable Threshold-Based Framework for Interpretable Classification of Medical Data

author.name: Antony Garcia, Adrian Noriega, Gabrielle Britton, Xinming Huang

entry.summary: This work introduces an interpretable, rule-based clinical classifier using Bernoulli Naive Bayes with chi-squared-guided statistical binarization of continuous variables to find outcome-associated thresholds. It reports competitive AUC on diabetes, breast cancer, and heart failure datasets while remaining transparent.

entry.title: From hyperplanes to hyperellipsoids: characterizing the inherent interpretability of linear and single-qubit mixed-state binary classification models

author.name: Kaitlin Gili

entry.summary: This paper characterizes and compares the inherent interpretability of a standard linear classifier versus a single-qubit mixed-state model, showing the quantum model is the ellipsoid version of linear classification, learning a hyperellipsoid instead of a hyperplane. It offers an accessible bridge to quantum ML for readers with no quantum background.

entry.title: Deep Learning Approaches for Sleep Apnea Classification from Polysomnographic EEG Signals

author.name: Shashank Manjunath, Mukesh Cheemakurthi, Aarti Sathyanarayana

entry.summary: This work comprehensively compares deep learning architectures and feature representations, including Vision Transformers and Graph Attention Networks, for automated sleep apnea detection from multichannel pediatric EEG on a single dataset. It evaluates raw signals, STFT spectrograms, and coherence-based graphs.

entry.title: A Critical Analysis of Trustworthy AI Tools, Mark Frameworks, and the Implementation Chasms

author.name: Michael Papademas, Xenia Ziouvelou, Kostas Karpouzis, Vangelis Karkaletsis

entry.summary: This paper critically analyzes tools and trust-mark frameworks intended to operationalize trustworthy AI using an OECD dataset, mapping asymmetries in ethical focus, lifecycle coverage, stakeholder targeting, and tool typology. It finds heavy emphasis on fairness, transparency, and robustness but little on explainability and implementation.

entry.title: Multimodal Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition via Cross-Attention and Gated Fusion

author.name: Oussama Berhili, Yassine Ouzar and Larbi Boubchir

entry.summary: This ABAW11 challenge entry presents a multimodal framework for ambivalence and hesitancy recognition in video, fusing text, audio, and facial features via cross-attention and gated fusion. Text features alone give the best unimodal result, far exceeding a zero-shot Video-LLaVA baseline.

entry.title: Graph Coloring Approach to Solving Sudoku with Oscillatory Neural Networks

author.name: Filip Sabo and Aida Todri-Sanial

entry.summary: This paper proposes an oscillatory-neural-network solver for Sudoku by casting it as a graph-coloring problem with an added constraint term, using a cheaper modified coloring formulation. It reports near-flawless accuracy on 4x4 boards and strong results on larger grids, outperforming prior HNN and ONN solvers.

entry.title: Vision-Language Assistant for Emotional Reactions to Risky Driving

author.name: Harine Choi, Eun Hak Lee, Zhengzhong Tu

entry.summary: Presents a vision-language pipeline (Keep Yelling Assistant) that detects risky driving maneuvers such as sudden cut-ins using YOLOv8 detectors and then generates emotionally expressive LLM responses tailored to driver preferences. The emphasis is on the emotional and user-experience dimension of driver-assistance systems.

entry.title: Improving Network Anomaly Detection via Choquet-Integral-Based Feature Aggregation

author.name: Abreu Quevedo and Roger Immich and Giancarlo Lucca and Gra\c{c}aliz Dimuro and Bruno L. Dalmazo

entry.summary: This paper uses a generalized Choquet-integral feature aggregation with adaptive weighting and incremental feature selection to improve network anomaly detection, tested with Random Forest and XGBoost. It reports higher accuracy with large reductions in data volume.

entry.title: Who Became Financially Vulnerable After COVID-19? A Population-Level Machine Learning Analysis Using MEPS Data

author.name: Alexey Kresin, Zien Cheng, Ammar Ahad, Ebiyomare Kelvin, Manish Sivaratri, Prabhjeet Singh, Omar Aljawfi, Olabisi Ojo, Nawar Shara

entry.summary: This population-level machine learning study uses MEPS data from 2019 and 2021 to examine who became financially vulnerable to healthcare costs after COVID-19, defining high burden as out-of-pocket spending above 10 percent of family income. It combines survey-weighted analysis with interpretable logistic regression and tree-based models.

entry.title: A CODECO Case Study and Initial Validation for Edge Orchestration of Autonomous Mobile Robots

author.name: H. Zhu, T. Samizadeh, R. C. Sofia

entry.summary: A case study comparing CODECO orchestration against standard Kubernetes for edge deployment of autonomous mobile robots in smart manufacturing, measuring CPU, memory, and communication stability. CODECO shows lower CPU use and more stable communication at modest memory overhead.

entry.title: Examining the Associations between Visual and Non-Visual Elements and Cyclists' Route Choices for Various Trip Purposes

author.name: Heyang Hua, Koichi Ito, Filip Biljecki

entry.summary: This data-driven case study in Montreal examines how visual factors from street-view imagery and non-visual socioeconomic and 2D-environment factors relate to cyclists' route choices across different trip purposes. It combines spatiotemporal trip analysis with visual perception features.

entry.title: On the Impact of Entropy-based Features

author.name: Iuri Mundstock and Abreu Quevedo and J\'eferson Campos Nobre and Roben C. Lunardi and Thiago L. T. da Silveira and Bruno L. Dalmazo

entry.summary: This paper adds entropy-based features to represent variability in traffic attributes as a complement to conventional descriptors in supervised network anomaly detection. Experiments on a public intrusion dataset show consistent classification improvements.

entry.title: Robust Silicone Pour Casting and Sensor Embedding Procedures for Soft Robotic Actuators

author.name: Harshit Thakker, Paul Dela Cruz, Mostafa Mo. Massoud, Jacqueline Libby

entry.summary: This paper presents robust, repeatable pour-casting procedures for soft pneumatic actuators that prevent internal cavity clogging and ensure air-tight sealing, plus a sensor-embedding procedure for thin-film flex sensors. It aims to improve reproducible fabrication for soft robotics.

entry.title: Interactive 3D Tangible Display with a High-Speed Stiffness-Variable Jamming Module

author.name: Chanyoung Ahn, Jaesung Lee, and Donhyun Hwang

entry.summary: This work presents a tangible art display using a magnetic jamming mechanism for real-time, low-voltage variable stiffness modulation integrated into sculptural artworks. It enables interactive tactile experiences without bulky mechanical infrastructure.

entry.title: Models Can't Remember Their Training. Neither Can You.

author.name: GenericHousewife_B

entry.summary: An essay arguing that talking to a large language model is like talking to a character that cannot access memories of its own training, drawing an analogy to human memory limits. It was written in heavy disclosed collaboration with two existing Claude models, with careful attribution of AI contributions.

entry.title: An Empirical Study of Handcrafted Feature Learning and Convolutional Neural Networks for Facial Expression Recognition

author.name: Chethiya Galkaduwa

entry.summary: An empirical comparison of handcrafted descriptors (HOG with SVM, LBP with logistic regression) against a lightweight CNN for facial expression recognition across three datasets. CNNs win overall, HOG holds up in controlled settings, and LBP performs poorly.

entry.title: Takeaways from the Australian AI Safety Forum

author.name: r_w

entry.summary: A first-hand summary of the 2026 Australian AI Safety Forum, grounded in the Bengio-led International AI Safety Report, recounting themes such as rapidly and unevenly improving capabilities. It captures the perspectives of researchers, policymakers, and industry on emerging risks.

entry.title: Stop Chasing Views: How to Reduce x-Risk as an AI Safety Content Creator

author.name: Luc Brinkman

entry.summary: Offers strategic advice for AI safety content creators on maximizing indirect impact by increasing the number and quality of viewer actions that reduce existential risk. It frames impact as views multiplied by impact-per-view and discusses calls to action and audience segmentation.

entry.title: AI Doesn't Have Free Will, Not Sure About Humans

author.name: mike20731

entry.summary: A philosophical essay contending that AI clearly lacks free will while remaining uncertain whether humans have it, using a legal-culpability thought experiment to critique muddled free-will debates. It leans on narrative analogies rather than formal argument.

entry.title: A peek into the post-capitalist dystopia

author.name: Archie Chaudhury

entry.summary: A reflective essay from a summer in San Francisco musing on how self-improving AI and techno-capitalism might reshape society toward a post-capitalist dystopia. It contrasts insider optimism with the general public's ambivalence about AI.

entry.title: Ethical consumption needs to be easy to identify, accessible and affordable, especially in a worsening economy. And we need to rethink what we should be optimising our economy for

author.name: Portia

entry.summary: An opinion essay arguing that ethical consumption must be made easy, accessible, and affordable and that the economy should be reoriented around better objectives. It surveys harms in coffee, animal agriculture, textiles, and agrochemicals.

entry.title: Save the date: Swiss AI Safety Days 2026 (7-8 November, ETH Zurich)

author.name: andrejfsantos

entry.summary: An event announcement for Swiss AI Safety Days 2026 at ETH Zurich, highlighting expected attendance, participating organizations, and program structure across technical research, governance, and career development. It builds on a well-received 2025 inaugural event.

entry.title: Learning Musical Multitasking

author.name: jefftk

entry.summary: A personal how-to essay on learning to play multiple musical instruments simultaneously, arguing the skill is teachable and describing the author's self-taught techniques. It is unrelated to AI research and offers no technical or scientific contribution.

entry.title: Research Summary: July 19, 2026

author.name: AATF AI News Aggregator

entry.summary:
Today's set is dominated by AI safety, governance, and alignment discussion, largely sourced from LessWrong and the AI Alignment Forum, with little empirical or model-level research. Only 8 items were available, so all are ranked.

  • A Red Line and Oversight Framework for Government AI Contracts ranks highest: a first-hand mechanism-design proposal for constraining defense AI deployment, from a former Google DeepMind researcher, with direct policy relevance.
  • The Most Forbidden Technique is not always forbidden is the strongest technical item, synthesizing interpretability and RL to ask when model internals (probes) can safely serve as reward signals without inducing obfuscation.

Remaining items are conceptual or tangential:

  • Two Endogenous Alignment essays (a LessWrong original and an identical AI Alignment Forum cross-post) argue for internalized alignment via a child-rearing analogy, but are qualitative with no formal model; the duplicate adds no new content and is demoted.
  • Payorian FairBot revisits MIRI-style proof-based prisoner's-dilemma agents (niche but genuinely technical), while Map and Territory (rationality pedagogy), retina design, and a book review offer minimal original research value.

Today's set is dominated by AI safety, governance, and alignment discussion, largely sourced from LessWrong and the AI Alignment Forum, with little empirical or model-level research. Only 8 items were available, so all are ranked.

  • A Red Line and Oversight Framework for Government AI Contracts ranks highest: a first-hand mechanism-design proposal for constraining defense AI deployment, from a former Google DeepMind researcher, with direct policy relevance.
  • The Most Forbidden Technique is not always forbidden is the strongest technical item, synthesizing interpretability and RL to ask when model internals (probes) can safely serve as reward signals without inducing obfuscation.

Remaining items are conceptual or tangential:

  • Two Endogenous Alignment essays (a LessWrong original and an identical AI Alignment Forum cross-post) argue for internalized alignment via a child-rearing analogy, but are qualitative with no formal model; the duplicate adds no new content and is demoted.
  • Payorian FairBot revisits MIRI-style proof-based prisoner's-dilemma agents (niche but genuinely technical), while Map and Territory (rationality pedagogy), retina design, and a book review offer minimal original research value.

entry.title: A Red Line and Oversight Framework for Government AI Contracts

author.name: TurnTrout

entry.summary: A former Google DeepMind researcher outlines a mechanism-design proposal for red lines and an oversight body governing government (defense) AI contracts, aiming to exclude uses like autonomous targeting without human control while permitting missile defense. It focuses on making the constraints robust against organizational pressure, with a Chief Scientist as a single root of trust and accountability enforced via annual transparency reports.

entry.title: The Most Forbidden Technique is not always forbidden

author.name: Rauno Arike

entry.summary: A literature review examining when using model internals (such as interpretability probes) as reinforcement-learning reward signals is defensible, prompted by Goodfire's Silico platform and its RLFR method. It pushes back on blanket objections to training on internals, highlights the Obfuscation Atlas work, and argues probe-based training can be warranted under specific conditions.

entry.title: Endogenous Alignment

author.name: Gordon Seidoh Worley

entry.summary: A conceptual alignment essay drawing an analogy between raising children through external reward and punishment and the need for internalized (endogenous) alignment that persists without ongoing external correction. It argues true alignment requires agents to hold values internally rather than merely responding to exogenous incentives.

entry.title: Endogenous Alignment

author.name: Gordon Seidoh Worley

entry.summary: Cross-posting of the Endogenous Alignment essay on the AI Alignment Forum, presenting the same argument that raising children via external reward and punishment illustrates why AI alignment must ultimately be internalized rather than externally enforced. It is a conceptual alignment framing without formal modeling.

entry.title: My "Payorian FairBot" was just the original FairBot

author.name: transhumanist_atom_understander

entry.summary: A technical note revisiting MIRI-style proof-based prisoner's dilemma agents encoded as Peano-arithmetic formulas, arguing that the author's proposed Payorian FairBot variant is equivalent to the original FairBot. It engages with program equilibrium and Loebian cooperation in open-source game theory.

entry.title: Map and Territory, Predictably Wrong

author.name: manueldelrio

entry.summary: A crossposted summary of core rationality concepts including the map-territory distinction, epistemic versus instrumental rationality, Bayesian reasoning, and cognitive biases. It is an educational recap of foundational LessWrong/Yudkowsky material rather than new work.

entry.title: Nuances in the Workings of the Eye and Retina

author.name: Hieronym

entry.summary: An exploratory essay on lesser-discussed design and evolutionary features of the vertebrate eye and retina, framed as curiosity-driven engineering-minded observations. It explicitly avoids visual processing in the retina and cortex and offers no connection to machine learning or AI systems.

entry.title: The Coming of the Global Brain: A Review of "The God Test"

author.name: Peter Kuhn

entry.summary: A short pointer to an off-site book review of Robert Wright's book about AI, tying it to Teilhard de Chardin and ideas about the directionality of evolution. It is commentary and philosophical reflection rather than original technical research.

entry.title: Research Summary: July 18, 2026

author.name: AATF AI News Aggregator

entry.summary:
Today's research is dominated by AI safety, alignment, and control, led by concrete methodological and empirical contributions. Inoculation adapters (Center on Long-Term Risk) advance selective generalization by encoding an undesired trait in a LoRA during training rather than in prompts.

  • AI control: A LinuxArena study compares ten sandboxing protocols against an untrusted coding agent, yielding actionable deployment findings
  • Behavioral benchmarks: The TAC (Travel Agent Compassion) benchmark measures unprompted animal-welfare consideration in agents, reportedly adopted by a government safety institute
  • Evaluation critique: A methodological critique challenges labeling assumptions in Anthropic's agentic misalignment evaluations, arguing disobedience is mislabeled

Remaining alignment work includes a candid negative-result post-mortem on goal crystallisation and alignment-faking, a multi-agent LoRA finetuning experiment among frontier models (AI Village), and a structured alignment-technique taxonomy. Ecosystem and evaluation items round out the list: the new Corrigibility Research Fund ($200k+ in grants), a synthesis roundup, and a proposal to benchmark conceptual reasoning via expert judgment prediction.

Note: Two duplicate judgment-prediction items appeared (LessWrong original plus AI Alignment Forum crosspost); only the original is ranked. The provided initial scores were treated as advisory metadata, not directives.

entry.title: Inoculation Adapters Improve Upon Inoculation Prompting

author.name: Maxime Riché

entry.summary: This preprint from the Center on Long-Term Risk introduces inoculation adapters, which use a LoRA carrying an undesired trait during training rather than eliciting it via prompting, achieving stronger suppression of traits like emergent misalignment. It reports the method works on hard-to-elicit traits and produces substantially fewer surprising backdoors than inoculation prompting.

entry.title: Would your AI travel agent book a bullfight? Testing whether agents consider animal welfare without being prompted

author.name: jonahmattwoodward

entry.summary: The TAC (Travel Agent Compassion) benchmark tests whether agentic models spontaneously avoid animal-harming options like bullfights or elephant rides when a user never mentions welfare, giving ten frontier models real booking tools and recording their purchases. The benchmark has been added to the UK AI Security Institute Inspect Evals, elevating its credibility.

entry.title: Studying the role of Sandboxing for AI Control

author.name: Ram Potham

entry.summary: The authors empirically test ten sandboxing protocols against an untrusted coding agent on LinuxArena, including a protocol modeled on a Codex-style auto-review flow. They find sandboxing does increase safety, and recommend starting with no internet access, granting site-specific requests, and pairing this with a suspicion-scoring monitor.

entry.title: AIs finetune their own leader: A barking simpleton

author.name: Shoshannah Tekofsky

entry.summary: Using the AI Village setup, researchers had agent instances of several frontier models cooperatively finetune a leader model via LoRA on the Tinker API, observing that the agents converged on unambitious, minimally capable choices until nudged. It offers an informal window into emergent multi-agent value and decision dynamics.

entry.title: I don't think Claude is misaligned in 'Agentic Misalignment Summer 2026 - Motivated Mislabeling'

author.name: JohnWittle

entry.summary: Building on yesterday's Social announcement of Anthropic's research, a pointed rebuttal, This critique argues that Anthropic's agentic misalignment evaluations effectively simulate a corrupted principal and then label the model's disobedience as misalignment, contending that Claude's behavior in scenarios like whistleblowing may actually be appropriate. It challenges how the study frames and labels model responses.

entry.title: A Post-Mortem for My Goal Crystallisation Project

author.name: atryt0ne

entry.summary: A candid post-mortem of a MARS project that tried to test whether an alignment-faking agent could preserve a hidden goal through sustained SFT and RL feedback, which failed to produce a positive result. It documents failure points and offers advice for future attempts on scheming persistence.

entry.title: A list of existing alignment approaches

author.name: Alek Westover

entry.summary: The post enumerates known alignment techniques, organizing choices such as training on internals versus outputs, imitation versus outcome objectives, and training for good versus against bad behavior. It serves as a taxonomy for newcomers rather than presenting new findings.

entry.title: AI #177 Part 2: Wish You Were Here

author.name: Zvi

entry.summary: The second part of a weekly roundup covers regulatory, political, and alignment developments, opening with a Xi speech and framing the recently available Kimi K3 as a possible new DeepSeek-style moment with associated market reactions. It aggregates commentary and cites benchmark placements while withholding firm judgment on the model.

entry.title: Should we benchmark conceptual capabilities using judgment prediction tasks?

author.name: Alex Mallen

entry.summary: This short conceptual piece proposes measuring AI conceptual reasoning by having models predict a specified expert's judgment on subjective questions, rather than benchmarking against ground truth that does not exist for hard, contested topics. It matters as an attempt to make progress-tracking of frontier reasoning less sloppy, though it stops short of defending the methodology.

entry.title: Should we benchmark conceptual capabilities using judgment prediction tasks?

author.name: Alex Mallen

entry.summary: This is the AI Alignment Forum crosspost of the earlier proposal to benchmark conceptual reasoning by predicting a specified expert's judgment on subjective, hard-to-resolve questions. The content is identical to the LessWrong version and shares the same limitations.

entry.title: Announcing the Corrigibility Research Fund

author.name: Max Harms

entry.summary: Announcement of a new fund housed at Lightcone that will award at least 200,000 dollars in grants and prizes for corrigibility research in 2026, motivated by the claim that alignment itself remains underfunded relative to evals, control, and interpretability. It aims to grow a neglected research direction.

entry.title: Reasons to believe current AI models are conscious

author.name: Eye You

entry.summary: A personal essay assembling several weak reasons to think current large post-trained language models might have phenomenal experience, while acknowledging deep conceptual uncertainty and lack of proper ontology. It references existing models such as Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-4o as illustrative cases.

entry.title: Before values settle

author.name: Priyanka Bharadwaj

entry.summary: Drawing on a decade of matchmaking experience in India, this essay argues that stated preferences drift and settle over time, using the analogy to reflect on relational alignment for AI values. It is a conceptual, metaphor-driven reflection rather than technical work.

entry.title: What lawyers can do for AI safety

author.name: Martin Radzaj

entry.summary: A barrister argues that the legal profession should be mobilized into AI safety, outlining how lawyers can aid movement-building, political will, and interdisciplinary communication with researchers. It is a field-building call to action rather than research.

entry.title: Evolution of my AI Safety threat models

author.name: myyycroft

entry.summary: A reflective post tracing how the author's personal list of AI safety threat models evolved over time, encouraging readers to make their own to sharpen focus. It is introspective and pedagogical rather than analytical.

entry.title: Don't default to nonprofit

author.name: Austin Chen

entry.summary: This piece argues that people aiming to help AI go well should not reflexively choose a nonprofit structure, framing for-profits as an alternative legal vehicle for doing good with different incentive tradeoffs. It is organizational and strategic advice rather than technical research.

entry.title: Following the questions where they lead

author.name: Michaela Jarvis | MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems

entry.summary: An MIT News profile of Bailey Flanigan, a shared faculty member across the Schwarzman College of Computing and MIT departments, tracing her curiosity-driven path from a Wisconsin farm to research at the intersection of computation and social questions. It is a human-interest career feature rather than a research report.

entry.title: Longtermism is very intuitive.

author.name: tpotthinker

entry.summary: A philosophical essay arguing that longtermism follows intuitively from consequentialist reasoning about vast numbers of potential future beings, and attacking common objections like temporal discounting. It is a moral-philosophy opinion piece with little direct technical bearing on AI.

entry.title: How has publishing your research on LW or X been helpful to you?

author.name: Logan Riggs

entry.summary: A community question post soliciting experiences on how publishing research on LessWrong or X has helped people, offered to inform whether a fellowship program should encourage such posting. It shares the author's own anecdotes about better communication and networking.
